items.rationale: The model was fit to the training data, so its accuracy there measures how well it learned rows it has already seen, not how it does on new data; that score is too optimistic.
An 80/20 split puts 20% of the rows in the test set: 0.20 x 1,000 = 200. The other 800 rows are the training set.

items.answer: How well the model will do on new data it has not seen during training.
accepted: How well the model performs on unseen data
How accurate the model will be on new data
How the model will do in the real world on data it was not trained on
items.rationale: A right answer says the test score estimates performance on new or unseen data; everyday wording such as 'in the real world' counts.
Choosing the model by its test score fits it a little to the test set each time, so the test set is no longer unseen and its score is too optimistic; those choices belong on a validation set.

items.answer: So the test score measures how the model does on new data it has never seen, instead of data it has already learned or memorized.
accepted: So the score shows performance on unseen data
So the model is evaluated on data it did not learn from
items.rationale: A full answer says what the test score then measures: performance on data the model has not seen. Saying only that it prevents cheating names the danger but not what the held-out data is for.
The test accuracy, 70%, is measured on data the model did not see, so it estimates performance on new data; the 99% training accuracy only shows how well the model fits data it has already learned.
